newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Hong Kong's consumers start spending again.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hong Kong's consumers start spending again.

text.p: Retail sales data released on Monday showed a second month of strong growth, showing Hong Kongers may be moving back to their old free-spending ways, analysts said.

The value of total retail sales in January was an estimated HK$22.1 billion, up 15 percent on the same month in 1996, according to provisional figures from the government, which warned, however, that the annual Chinese Lunar New Year festival can introduce volatility into the figures.
Sales rose 10 percent in inflation-adjusted volume terms.
Hong Kong consumers invested in consumer durables like motor vehicles in January, with sales volume and value surging by 71 percent year-on-year, according to the government.
Purchases of valuable goods -- jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts -- grew 17 percent by value and 20 percent by volume compared to the same month in 1996, it said.
In December, retail sales rose eight percent by value and three percent by volume on the year, compared to gains of 6.3 percent by value and 1.6 percent by volume for 1996 as a whole.

Analysts said the latest numbers hinted at recovery after months of soft consumer demand and political uncertainty. Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule.

The data made welcome reading after a long period of stagnant consumer demand and relatively high unemployment as the economy grew just 4.7 percent in both 1995 and 1996 compared to the 10-year average of 5.9 percent.
Merrill Lynch economist Nicholas Kwan described the data as very strong, and signs the local economy was off its lows.
Rob Gvozden, an economist at Lehman Brothers, said he had noticed "fairly robust purchases of consumer durables".
He had been waiting for lagging indicators like inflation and employment numbers to get an idea of the trend in the Hong Kong economy and consumer activities.
Unemployment in the three months to February 1997 was 2.4 percent, down from 3.2 percent in the January 1996 quarter, and 1996 inflation was six percent, versus 8.2 percent in 1995.
Gvozden downplayed the impact of the July 1 handover on consumer spending patterns.
"Our feeling is that the factors surrounding the transition (to Chinese rule) -- at least in terms of sentiment -- are really of minimal weight in people's decisions," Govzden said.

Hong Kong Trade Development Council Michael Martin of the Trade Development Council said people appeared to be more confident now that China and Britain were resolving outstanding (Sino-British) issues "one way or the other".
"It's easier to live with a 'yes' or a 'no' than 'maybe'," Martin said.
However, SBC Warburg Securities' Simon Ogus warned against reading too much into the sales figures in terms of long-term trends, and consumer confidence.
"To be honest, if we see capital movement out of Hong Kong, it doesn't have to happen now," Ogus said.
Ian Perkin, Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce chief economist, also sounded a cautionary note, saying any recovery in consumer demand and sales was still patchy.
-- Sean Kennedy Hong Kong newsroom (852) 2843 6321
